title: Khumi Chin Community Opposes AA’s Arakan Language Curriculum in Paletwa
body:
Indigenous Khumi Chin leaders and civil society groups have strongly opposed the Arakan Army’s (AA) implementation of an Arakan-language curriculum in basic education schools across Chin State’s Paletwa Township, calling the move a violation of indigenous rights.
The controversy arose after the AA and its political wing, the United League of Arakan (ULA), introduced Arakanese literature and history as a mandatory Grade 12 subject for the current academic year—replacing the standard Myanmar language subject not only in controlled areas of Arakan (Rakhine) State, but also in neighboring Paletwa.
In a statement issued on September 6, the Global Khumi Organization (GKO) condemned the policy, stating that imposing an external ethnic curriculum without local consent violates the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and risks sowing deep communal divisions.
"Bringing a new Arakan-language curriculum into Paletwa, which is an integral part of Chin State, is seen as an attempt to exert dominant ethnic influence," a local Khumi resident told Chin World. "People are only remaining quiet because those issuing the orders are armed."
Developed by the ULA’s Arakan National Education Department, the new Grade 12 curriculum uses the Myanmar alphabet to teach Arakanese literature, history, and traditional customs.
While Khumi literature is already taught in predominantly Khumi areas, local communities view the AA's unilateral educational policy as an overreach of authority in Chin State, underscoring growing governance tensions between the regional resistance administration and local ethnic minorities.

title: Scammers Target Myanmar Travelers in Shan State to Fuel Telecom Fraud Operations
body:
Fraudsters in southern Shan State’s Taunggyi Township are targeting travelers at intercity bus stops and transit hubs, posing as bank representatives to collect national identification card (NIC) data and facial photographs for telecom scam syndicates, according to residents and victims.
Operating in towns like Aungpan, middle-aged scammers lure unsuspecting victims with offers to set up free accounts at major financial institutions, including KBZ Bank and AYA Bank.
After they take photographs of victims' identity cards and faces, the perpetrators abscond, selling the biometric and personal data to online scam operations—locally known as Zhapaian—for tens of millions of Myanmar kyat.
The scam exploits military junta travel mandates that require Myanmar citizens to carry physical identity cards at all times due to ongoing political instability.
Most victims realize their information has been stolen when they attempt to open a bank account themselves.
A resident of neighboring Ywangan Township, for instance, was turned away by KBZ Bank staff after finding an account had already been fraudulently registered using his identity credentials.
"I was in Aungpan when people offered to help me open a bank account. They took photos of my NIC and face, then claimed they couldn't finish it right away and left," the victim told the Shan Herald Agency for News. "When I later went to open an account myself, I was told one was already registered under my name."DOCX
Community members and cybersecurity advocates warn that stolen credentials put victims at severe legal risk, exposing them to liabilities involving illicit financial transactions, money laundering, and unauthorized loans.
Concerns are also growing over parallel security threats on regional transit routes, where individuals in junta uniforms have reportedly been seen photographing travelers' identity documents.
Local tech advocates have additionally urged the public to beware of phishing links distributed via Viber and Telegram platforms used to compromise mobile devices.

title: Key Myanmar Bridge Damaged in Junta Airstrike Amid Heavy Fighting Near Bhamo
body:
A strategic dual-use bridge in Kachin State’s Bhamo Township was damaged in a military junta airstrike on September 5, following heavy attacks by resistance forces on a military flotilla navigating the Ayeyarwady River, residents and resistance sources reported.
The Hsinhkan Bridge—which carries both a road and railway line linking Bhamo with Katha in Sagaing Region—sustained structural damage during the bombardment. The airstrike bent the supporting steel frame on the eastern side, left a car-sized crater in the bridge deck, and rendered the railway line completely unusable.
The attack occurred after a 15-vessel junta flotilla traveling upstream from Mandalay came under intense ambush by a resistance coalition, including the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and the Kachin People’s Defence Force (KPDF).
“The junta bombed the bridge both to secure the flotilla’s passage and to sever logistics routes coming from Sagaing Region,” a Bhamo-based resistance fighter stated on social media, noting that the narrow river section near Hsinhkan Village is a frequent ambush site.
While parts of the flotilla were heavily damaged—leading to the surrender of several vessels and the capture of nearly 200 prisoners of war by the KIA—seven ships, including two combat vessels, managed to reach Bhamo Town. Other vessels remain stranded in Shwegu Township.
Ground fighting continues to rage around Hsinhkan, Waema, Sinsakhan, and Nawngmo villages as disembarked junta troops attempt to regroup and counter resistance forces. Ongoing hostilities have restricted access to the site, preventing independent verification of the full extent of the bridge's damage.

title: Heavy Fighting Enters Fourth Day as Myanmar Junta Tries to Advance Along Sittwe-Ponnagyun Border
body:
Intense clashes between Myanmar military junta forces and the Arakan Army (AA) continued for a fourth consecutive day on September 7 along the border of Sittwe and Ponnagyun townships, as junta troops attempted to push deeper into AA-controlled territory, according to military sources and local reports.
Fighting escalated on the morning of September 4 when junta ground forces, supported by armored vehicles and naval warships, launched an offensive across the strategic Minchaung Bridge toward Kuntaung village in Ponnagyun Township.
The Arakan Army subsequently deployed reinforcements and launched counterattacks.
Over the past four days, the junta has unleashed heavy artillery, drone strikes, and jet fighter bombardments targeting civilian communities across Ponnagyun, Rathedaung, and Pauktaw townships. Affected areas include Kuntaung, Sabahtar, Aidin, Thonesaung, Phetkya, and Thaekhon villages, causing significant destruction and damaging civilian property.
"From around 1:00 PM on September 6, the Arakan Army launched drone attacks near Minchaung Bridge, followed by intermittent exchanges of heavy artillery and small-arms fire throughout the day," a military source told DMG.
Military analysts view the offensive across Minchaung Bridge as a strategic attempt by the military regime to establish a foothold in Ponnagyun Township and secure key transport junctions leading to Rathedaung.
"Their primary objective is Minchaung Bridge and Kuntaung village, aiming to secure control up to the Ponnagyun-Rathedaung road junction," said Captain Zin Yaw, a military defector.
The ongoing escalation has forced thousands of civilians from roughly 20 villages across Ponnagyun and Rathedaung townships to flee their homes.
Simultaneous conflict is escalating elsewhere in Arakan State. Heavy fighting continues in Kyaukphyu Township amid junta naval movements and ground advances, while junta forces are attempting amphibious landings supported by relentless airstrikes in Thandwe and Gwa townships.
Analysts warn that hostilities across the region are likely to intensify further as the junta deploys massive air, naval, and ground assets in a bid to reclaim territory lost to the Arakan Army.

title: Myanmar Junta Arrests Married Couple in Mon State Over Alleged Links to Resistance Groups
body:
Myanmar military junta forces have arrested a married couple in Mon State’s Thanbyuzayat Township for allegedly supplying information to anti-junta resistance forces, according to residents and sources close to the police.
The couple—identified as 31-year-old Aung Myint Mo Htet (also known as Maung Phyu) and his wife, Ma Phyu Phyu Aung (also known as Ma Phyu)—were detained around noon on September 4 while working as rubber tappers in the Peinhnetaw village area.
Sources close to local law enforcement said the migrant couple was targeted for allegedly reporting military troop movements to joint Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) and People’s Defense Force (PDF) units, as well as failing to report resistance activity to junta authorities.
“They were arrested because they were reportedly providing information to revolutionary groups about the movements and activities of the military,” a resident told Mon News.
The couple is currently being held at Thanbyuzayat Police Station and faces prosecution under Section 52(a) of the Counter-Terrorism Law, a charge that carries severe prison sentences.
The arrests reflect a broader ongoing crackdown across Mon State, where junta forces routinely detain civilians on suspicion of aiding revolutionary groups. In August, three residents were similarly charged under the Counter-Terrorism Law merely for posting comments on social media pages associated with resistance organizations.

title: At Least Five Dead, Including Two Children, as Severe Flooding Hits Myanmar’s Kale Township
body:
Severe flooding triggered by torrential rainfall and mountain runoff in Sagaing Region’s Kale Township—located near the border with India—has killed at least five people, including two children, and displaced more than 1,000 residents, according to local rescue teams and officials.
Days of heavy rain and runoff from the neighboring Chin Hills caused the Myittha River and local creeks to overflow last week, submerging low-lying wards and surrounding villages, including Nat Chaung, Aung Myin Thar, Sae Gyi, Nat Nan, and Zin Ka Lin.
Floodwaters have begun to recede, but local authorities and rescue groups warn that thick layers of mud and the threat of waterborne diseases, such as diarrhea and skin infections, pose ongoing risks to survivors.
Among the victims was 15-year-old Maung Aung Phway Win, who drowned on September 6 after being swept away by strong currents in Thwi Ngoe Creek while retrieving floating firewood with his father.
Other casualties include a young child who died in a landslide on September 3 while watching floodwaters in Kale’s 9-Mile area, a 55-year-old woman swept away after a riverbank collapsed near U-pot Creek, a 28-year-old cattle herder in Letpanchaung village, and an unidentified man whose body was recovered near Chan Thar village.
Over 1,000 displaced residents are currently taking temporary shelter in local schools across Kale town as authorities assess the damage to homes and agricultural land.
Myanmar’s Department of Meteorology and Hydrology had previously reported that the Myittha River crested nearly two feet above its danger mark before water levels began to fall over the weekend.

title: Arakan Ethnic Media Outlet Narinjara News Marks 25 Years Amid Press Freedom Crisis
body:
Independent media organization Narinjara News marked its 25th anniversary on September 7, celebrating a major milestone as one of Arakan’s longest-running ethnic news outlets operating amid severe political instability and safety threats across Myanmar.
Founded on September 7, 2001, Narinjara has spent a quarter-century reporting on political, social, and humanitarian affairs in Arakan State, navigating successive periods of military rule, democratic transition, and intense armed conflict.
The outlet’s 25-year journey mirrors the broader evolution of Myanmar’s ethnic press, growing from early publications such as Arakan Post to key partnerships with regional ethnic media networks.
However, the anniversary comes at a perilous moment for press freedom in Myanmar. Since the 2021 military coup, independent journalists have faced unprecedented risks, including armed violence, junta airstrikes, widespread displacement, telecommunications blackouts, and severe access restrictions.
The media landscape in Arakan State has shifted dramatically as the United League of Arakan/Arakan Army (ULA/AA) expands its territorial control.
At the same time, active fighting persists in remaining junta-held enclaves.
Media observers emphasize that independent reporting remains vital during conflict and political transition to document humanitarian conditions, civilian protection, and human rights, while holding both military and newly emerging governing structures accountable.
Narinjara’s silver jubilee highlights the enduring resilience of ethnic media in giving local communities a voice and providing crucial public access to reliable information despite mounting danger.

title: Woman Injured in Junta Artillery Shelling in Southern Myanmar
body:
A 38-year-old woman was injured when an artillery shell fired by Myanmar military junta forces struck a residential area in Tanintharyi Region’s Yebyu Township, according to residents and news reports.
The incident occurred early on September 3 following a 30-minute clash between revolutionary forces and an advancing junta column moving from Kywetalin village toward Yar Phue village.
Following the engagement, junta forces fired two artillery shells toward the surrounding communities.
One shell detonated at a cemetery outside Kywetalin village, while the second hit a home at the entrance of Yar Phue village, wounding the victim in the hand with shrapnel.
“They fired two artillery shells indiscriminately after the gunfire stopped,” a resident told Mon News. “That’s how a woman was struck in the hand. Fortunately, her injuries were not life-threatening.”
The victim is currently receiving medical treatment at a local village clinic.
The attack comes amid a significant military buildup in the area. Local sources report that the junta deployed over 100 additional troops to Yar Phue and Kywetalin during the final week of August, doubling the total visible force to over 200 soldiers, excluding roving patrols in nearby forests.
The motive behind the deployment remains unclear, as no prior clashes had been reported in the days leading up to the reinforcement.
Human rights advocates have repeatedly documented military atrocities in the region. According to a recent report by Fortify Rights, junta forces in Yebyu Township have engaged in killings, torture, and the arson of civilian homes as part of efforts to secure control over the strategic Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ).

title: Myanmar Junta Bans Villagers in Mandalay’s Myingyan District from Buying Rice
body:
Military junta forces in central Myanmar have banned residents from surrounding villages from entering key towns in Mandalay Region’s Myingyan District to purchase food and medicine, according to residents and an activist group.
The ban applies to major commercial hubs in the district, including Myingyan, Taungtha, and Natogyi Towns.
Locals reported that junta troops and members of the allied Pyusawhti militia at entry and exit checkpoints are confiscating basic supplies, physically assaulting buyers, and threatening them with death if they attempt to transport goods back to their villages.
The restrictions began in Myingyan and Taungtha on September 5, and extended to Natogyi on September 7, according to local sources and the Myingyan Public Movement Committee.
“They strictly prohibit us from bringing back rice, cooking oil, or medicine,” a Myingyan resident told Mizzima. “They told us, ‘Do not come at all. If you return, we will shoot you dead.’ All roads linking the towns and villages are now blocked.”DOCX
Sources indicate the travel ban could remain in place for 10 to 15 days, mimicking the military's long-standing "Four Cuts" doctrine—a counter-insurgency strategy designed to sever food, funding, intelligence, and recruitment lines to resistance forces.
Checkpoint inspections have grown increasingly violent. Residents carrying more than 4.2 kilograms of rice are reportedly physically assaulted, while those carrying smaller quantities have their food confiscated and discarded.
The restrictions pose a severe threat to food security in Myingyan District. Located in Myanmar’s arid Dry Zone, the area relies heavily on imported rice from irrigated regions like Ayeyarwady and Sagaing.
Local farmers primarily cultivate cash crops such as pulses, sesame, cotton, and onions, producing very little rice of their own.
While the junta has restricted the movement of food, oil, and salt in Myingyan District since last year—often subjecting villagers to extortion and transit fees of up to 5,000 MMK ($2.30 USD) per bag of rice—the complete closure of access roads marks a sharp escalation in enforcement.

title: Child Killed, Woman Injured in Junta Artillery Attack on Mon State Village
body:
A 10-year-old child was killed and his mother injured when Myanmar military junta forces shelled a civilian village in Mon State’s Bilin Township without prior engagement, according to residents.
Units from the junta’s Light Infantry Division 44, based in neighboring Kyaikto Township, fired two artillery shells toward Nyaung Thoke village at around 5:00 p.m. on September 6.
One shell detonated inside the village, killing the 10-year-old child instantly. The victim's mother, a woman in her 40s, suffered shrapnel wounds and is receiving care.
“The child was killed on the spot when the shell landed, and the mother was injured,” a resident told Mon News, emphasizing that no active fighting was occurring in or around the village at the time of the attack.
The shelling marks the latest in a series of indiscriminate attacks targeting civilian areas in Bilin Township. In August, a similar junta artillery strike in Zee Pyaw village killed a five-year-old kindergarten student and wounded at least 11 others.
According to reports from the Karen National Union (KNU), the military regime has increasingly relied on heavy artillery and airstrikes against populated villages across the region, resulting in rising civilian casualties, widespread destruction of homes, and the displacement of thousands of residents.

title: Junta Deputy Commander Calls for Integrity, but Reality Tells a Different Story
body:
Although the junta’s deputy commander-in-chief has called on military officers leading battalions and brigades to avoid misconduct and uphold integrity, the reality on the ground is starkly different, according to Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM) participants and residents.
On September 4, during a meeting with officers at the Army’s Defense Services Headquarters compound in Naypyitaw, junta Deputy Commander-in-Chief General Kyaw Swar Lin stressed the importance of integrity and ethical conduct.
In his speech, he urged officers to set an example by adhering strictly to military discipline and warning against illicit drugs, corruption, sexual misconduct, and online gambling. In practice, however, systemic corruption reportedly permeates every level of the Myanmar military.
Captain Zin Yaw, a former military officer who joined the CDM, noted that some senior officers accumulated wealth through illegal drug trafficking early in their careers as second lieutenants before rising to high-ranking positions at headquarters. Consequently, leadership is fully aware of illicit activities by lower-level officers.
“The junta’s unwritten rule is that wrongdoing isn’t considered a crime unless you get caught,” Captain Zin Yaw said. “Even when someone is exposed, senior officers usually shield those close to them. The system doesn't deter misconduct—it simply encourages personnel to do it covertly.”
Illicit trade, drug trafficking, and online gambling operations currently thrive across major cities. Meanwhile, junta checkpoints along the Thai-Myanmar border systematically extort money from merchants under the guise of enforcing trade regulations.
A local political analyst emphasized that junta officials and soldiers—from border security commanders to rank-and-file personnel—are deeply entangled in corruption networks, as cyber-scam hubs, human organ trafficking, and drug rings rely directly on military protection and kickbacks.
“None of them, from high-level border officers to frontline soldiers, are clean,” the analyst said. “Virtually all illegal operations function through direct ties to junta authorities. The military regime is the central hub and primary perpetrator of these criminal networks.”
Residents also report that rank-and-file soldiers, heavily addicted to online gambling, routinely extort money and confiscate civilian property under pretenses.
“Soldiers at the bottom level are addicted to online gambling,” a border resident told Than Lwin Times. “They accuse civilians of carrying illegal goods, seize the items, and then erase them from official records. Ordinary people bear the brunt of this unchecked corruption.”
Furthermore, junta troops have reportedly been selling goods confiscated during raids on telecom scam centers along the Thai border at steep discounts and dividing the proceeds among themselves—a practice senior administrative officials are fully aware of but willfully ignore.

title: Four Rakhine IDPs Killed in Ayeyarwady Region Airstrikes Within a Month
body:
Two displaced Rakhine civilians were killed on September 5 during a military airstrike on Pantawgyi village in Lay Myint Township, Ayeyarwady Region, according to local sources.
The victims—a father and son who had previously fled conflict in Rakhine State—were identified as U Hla Shwe, over 60, and Ko Min Htwe, over 30.
Residents reported that a military aircraft bombed the village around 5:00 a.m. despite the absence of active clashes in the immediate area. The strike destroyed at least six homes belonging to both residents and displaced families.
“Pantawgyi is located right on the Rakhine State border,” a resident told Narinjara. “There is no active fighting or military presence here. These families fled the war in Rakhine because they had nowhere else to go. They were already struggling with severe food shortages and poor living conditions, and now they are being bombed. The area is cut off from communications, and the remaining displaced people don't know where to run next.”
Pantawgyi village sits along the border between Ayeyarwady Region and the Rakhine Yoma mountain range—a strategic frontier where both the Arakan Army (AA) and its allies, as well as junta troops, maintain an active presence.
This attack marks the second fatal bombing of Rakhine refugees in the region within a single month. On August 5, a military airstrike targeted Thae Phyu village in neighboring Tharbaung Township—another border zone near the Rakhine Yoma—killing two displaced brothers and destroying their home.
The victims of that attack were identified as Ko Nga Soe, 40, and Ko Hla Htwe, 30, who had originally fled Gwa Township in Rakhine State.

title: Women Group Calls for Urgent, Concrete Action to End Myanmar Junta Violence Against Civilians
body:
As violence and human rights violations committed by the Myanmar military continue to escalate nationwide, the Burmese Women’s Union (BWU) has urgently called for precise and concrete international action to end atrocities against civilians.
According to a report released by the BWU on September 4, at least 55 women—including six minors—were killed in August 2026 alone due to military airstrikes, heavy artillery shelling, gunfire, and landmines.
Ma Yin Myo Hlaing, Joint General Secretary 1 of the BWU, emphasized that women and children are bearing the brunt of the military's direct targeting of civilian areas, underscoring the vital need for effective interventions.
“To prevent further loss of innocent lives and achieve the democracy we desire, we want a transition with reduced conflict and violence,” Ma Yin Myo Hlaing said. “A robust mechanism must be established to ensure full accountability for victims of violence, and concrete measures are essential to deliver justice.”
To support survivors and victims, the BWU is actively documenting and publishing evidence of abuses while delivering emergency assistance, including healthcare, food aid, and mental health referrals.
The organization's August data reveals that casualty rates among women were highest in Rakhine (Arakan) State with 17 fatalities, followed by Sagaing Region with 13. Other reported female deaths include nine in Chin State, six in Magway Region, three each in Bago Region and Karenni State, two in Kayin State, and one each in Mandalay and Tanintharyi regions.
Human rights advocates have strongly condemned the junta for weaponizing its air superiority against civilian populations amid mounting battlefield losses.
“I urge the international community to take effective action against the military regime for its ongoing crimes, human rights violations, and breaches of the Geneva Conventions,” said U Myat Tun, Director of the Arakan Human Rights Defenders and Promoters Association (AHRDPA). “They must swiftly face justice before the International Criminal Court (ICC) and International Court of Justice (ICJ).”
According to BWU documentation, military air and ground operations between January and July 2026 resulted in 358 female deaths and injured 351 others across Myanmar.

title: Myanmar Junta Struggles to Establish Control in Chin State Despite Retaking Several Towns
body:
Although the Myanmar military has retaken several towns in Chin State, its administrative reach remains severely limited; Chin resistance organizations continue to control the vast majority of the territory, according to the Chinland Council.
Officials from the resistance-led Chinland Council shared this assessment during a press conference on August 28 following the release of their report, “Building Chinland: Exercising Self-Determination – Two and a Half Years of Alternative Governance by the Chinland Council.”
“Even previously, the junta’s influence in Chin State was confined to urban pockets in select townships, with no real authority over rural areas,” said Dr. Sui Khar, Foreign Minister of the Chinland Council-run Government of Chinland. “Official directives from the regime simply could not reach those regions. "Recently, the junta managed to retake towns such as Tonzang and Falam, but it still struggles to secure them. The regime is primarily focused on controlling key transit routes, such as the highways connecting Kalay in Sagaing Region with Hakha and Tedim in Chin State; it has failed to gain total control."
To secure the Kalay–Tedim and Kalay–Hakha highways, the military has established over 30 outposts and garrisons along the routes—an unprecedented deployment that highlights its precarious grip on the roads rather than firm control.
While the junta has reclaimed most parts of Falam, Tonzang, and Thantlang—towns previously liberated by resistance forces—it has been unable to restore its administrative machinery.
“The limits of the regime’s administrative reach were clearly exposed when it had to exclude numerous areas from its election,” said Salai Kep Chin Thang, secretary of the Chinland Council. “This demonstrates that the military still lacks total control. We retain the capacity to challenge them militarily at any time while maintaining parallel influence even within junta-controlled urban centers. In short, we continue to exert pressure through both military operations and governance.”
Across Chin State, the military’s administrative apparatus functions only in isolated urban centers. In contrast, Chin resistance forces continue to administer most of the territory, including vast rural areas and villages.
“While a few cities, towns, and their immediate surroundings remain under Naypyidaw’s control, the regime’s influence elsewhere is practically non-existent,” Dr. Sui Khar added. “Across those vast rural spans and liberated towns, the Chinland Council leads and operates the administrative system.”
Since the 2021 military coup, the junta has faced widespread armed resistance across Myanmar. In Chin State, various resistance groups initially captured numerous towns and established local governance structures.
Although the regime has launched counter-offensives to retake strategically vital territories, the majority of Chin State remains firmly under resistance control.

title: Indo-Myanmar Border Fencing Reaches 55 km, Full Completion Targeted for 2028
body:
Approximately 55 kilometers of the border fence along India’s Manipur State and Myanmar has been completed, with the entire stretch targeted for completion by 2028, Manipur State Home Minister Govindas Konthoujam announced on September 2.
The minister disclosed the details in the State Legislative Assembly during a response to a calling attention motion raised by opposition MLA K. Ranjit Singh regarding reports of a proposed India-Myanmar land exchange.
Addressing the assembly, the Home Minister stated that the Manipur state government has not received any official communication from the Ministry of External Affairs regarding a land swap.
He emphasized that the government must consult affected residents before making decisions regarding territorial sovereignty.
Reports surfaced that the Indian government proposed a boundary adjustment involving approximately 1.4 square miles of land between border pillars 65 and 68, situated between Manipur’s Chandel district, India, and the Kabaw Valley in Sagaing Region, Myanmar.
The reports, initially published by The Diplomat on July 17, followed a visit to India by Myanmar Junta leader Min Aung Hlaing from May 30 to June 3, during which border security issues were discussed.
The minister explained that Manipur shares a 398-kilometer border with Myanmar, spanning from border pillars 32 to 130, with fencing currently completed along roughly 55 kilometers.
He highlighted the Moreh sector, between border pillars 75 and 79, as a vital and sensitive strategic area.
He added that logistics and difficulties in transporting construction materials have delayed the project, while demarcation work on remaining unmarked border stretches is ongoing.
However, resistance forces on the Myanmar side have voiced opposition to the project. A representative from the Tamu Township People’s Defense Force (PDF) told Mizzima that border fencing cannot be executed unilaterally, especially in undemarcated areas where territorial disputes persist.
“The fencing issue cannot be resolved unilaterally,” the PDF member said. “There are undemarcated territories and instances of encroachment. Fencing should not be forced through at this time and should only proceed after consulting a democratically elected government and gaining the agreement of local communities.”
According to the PDF representative, at least six instances of territorial encroachment from the Indian side have been documented.
Local PDF units have organized protests at active construction sites, including areas near Myothit town in upper Tamu Township, the Moreh-Tamu corridor, and stretches near border pillars 59–60, 75–76, and 82–83.
The representative also cited an unresolved incident near border pillar 59, alleging that Indian military personnel crossed into Myanmar, raided a Tamu District People’s Defense Team (PDT/PaKaPha) camp, and killed 10 members.
India is currently working to fence its entire 1,643-kilometer border with Myanmar to curb drug trafficking, illegal trade, undocumented migration, refugee spillovers, armed conflict, and broader security threats.
Despite New Delhi's security push, indigenous communities along the border—including the Mizo, Naga, Kuki, and Zo populations—continue to oppose the barrier.
They argue that a physical fence divides indigenous ancestral lands, disrupts local agricultural livelihoods, and severs shared ethnic and cultural ties.
