title: Military Offensive in Southern Ponnagyun Halts Following Heavy Casualties
body:
A major military offensive in southern Ponnagyun Township, located 16 miles north of the Rakhine State capital of Sittwe, has reportedly ground to a halt after junta forces suffered heavy casualties, according to local sources.
The multi-pronged assault, which began on September 4, involved coordinated operations from the army, navy, and air force.
“The military attacked several villages controlled by the Arakan Army (AA) in southern Ponnagyun Township,” a local military source told Narinjara. “They carried out heavy airstrikes and naval shelling alongside a ground push. However, the military was forced to retreat in several areas due to severe casualties, and the offensive is currently stalled.”
Junta forces targeted AA-held villages from positions including Shwe Min Gan, Tow Kan, Ye Yo Pyin, Wa Bo, Ywa Haung Chaung, and Min Chaung, with the most intense clashes occurring near Shwe Min Gan.
“The navy advanced along the Kaladan River to shell the area, supported by aircraft, while ground columns advanced toward Shwe Min Gan and Tow Kan,” the source added. “As they pushed through Shwe Min Gan, AA forces engaged them at close range, inflicting heavy casualties.”
Reports indicate that the majority of junta casualties were newly conscripted militia members from the Regional Production Corps (RPCs).
“On the night of September 4, they bombed Min Hla village and fired heavy artillery before advancing toward AA positions,” another local source reported. “The AA fiercely retaliated. Many conscripts were killed because they lacked proper combat training. Local reports noted they were shot immediately upon raising their heads as they didn't even know how to crawl for cover.”
Concurrently, junta forces launched an assault north of the Min Chaung Bridge with naval and air support. However, local military sources confirmed they retreated to the bridge after suffering severe losses. Following the retreat, Sittwe-based military units targeted the outskirts of Kwan Taung village with artillery and drones.
Residents noted unconfirmed reports that the Arakan Army also suffered casualties during the clashes; however, the AA has not yet released an official statement.
“The AA initially withdrew from a small outpost near Kwan Taung due to being outnumbered,” a resident explained. “However, they quickly regrouped and counterattacked, forcing the military to retreat with heavy losses. AA forces also maintained the upper hand near Sapa Htar village, where junta troops suffered heavy casualties before falling back.”
While ground operations have paused following the military's retreat, naval vessels and Sittwe-based artillery units continue to launch intermittent shelling into southern Ponnagyun Township.
Narinjara is continuing to monitor the situation along the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border and will provide updates as more information becomes available.Photo: Crd

title: Thousands Flee Ponnagyun and Rathedaung as Fighting Escalates Near Sittwe
body:
Thousands of residents from Ponnagyun and Rathedaung townships, which border the Rakhine State capital of Sittwe, have been forced to flee their homes as heavy fighting intensifies, according to local sources.
Villagers reported that the Myanmar military has launched relentless strikes using heavy artillery, airstrikes, and rocket salvoes, impacting residential areas and causing civilian casualties.
“Artillery shells landed in Kuntaung, Padetha, and Yarchaung villages, as well as Ponnagyun Town,” said a female resident from Ponnagyun. “Residents in Yarchaung and Yayphyukan villages, along with people in Ponnagyun Town, have begun fleeing to safer areas after an exploding shell injured a woman on September 4.”
In Ponnagyun Township, displaced residents include locals from Tabethlan, Yarchaung, Ahtelthae, Hsininngyi, Yayphyukan, and Chaungwa Villages, as well as Ponnagyun Town itself.
Concurrently, hundreds of residents from Rathedaung Township—specifically Aungseik, Thanchaung, Kalarchaung, Aungma, Magyichaung, Angumaw, Kyetyoeseik, and Sarpyingyi Villages—are fleeing due to nearby clashes and the ongoing threat of junta artillery fire.
“Heavy artillery shells and small arms fire have been landing in the fields near our villages, leaving behind unexploded ordnance,” a local man from Rathedaung said. “Terrified by the constant gunfire, residents are seeking refuge in neighboring villages or staying with relatives.”
Intense clashes between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army (AA) have raged along the Sittwe-Ponnagyun border since September 4 and remain ongoing.
Amid relentless artillery fire from naval vessels and nine Sittwe-based battalions, the Arakan Army temporarily closed the main highway near Ponnagyun Town.
“Fighting remained intense this morning following overnight artillery and airstrikes,” a local man in Ponnagyun reported. “Shells landed directly on and near the highway, forcing a complete road closure. The military is firing indiscriminately.”
Clashes across Rakhine State have simultaneously escalated in the remaining junta-held hubs of Sittwe and Kyaukphyu, with the military relying heavily on air and naval power. Junta forces are also attempting amphibious landings along the coast in southern Rakhine's Gwa and Thandwe townships.

title: Retreating junta column hits landmines in Chaung-U after weeklong offensive
body:
A Myanmar military junta column of roughly 300 troops retreated from Chaung-U Township in Sagaing Region on September 3, leaving behind civilian casualties and looted villages before suffering heavy losses from landmines, according to local resistance sources.
Following the junta's withdrawal, revolutionary forces entered the affected villages to conduct clearance operations. During the sweep, fighters discovered the decomposing bodies of three residents alongside dead livestock.
“The bodies were already decomposing when we arrived,” a military source with the resistance forces said. “I urge residents to flee immediately as soon as they hear reports of an advancing column. Seeing civilians killed like this fills us with grief and anger. They had time to evacuate, but unfortunately stayed behind.”
Mizzima is currently verifying the identities and circumstances surrounding the three deceased residents.
According to resistance sources, the retreating troops heavily plundered civilian properties before hitting landmine traps laid by revolutionary forces along their withdrawal route.
“On their way back after looting, they detonated landmines planted along their path,” the source added. “Casualties appear to be high, and ambulances were seen rushing back and forth in chaos.”
The junta column originally launched its offensive on August 29, triggering a one-hour firefight with resistance forces on September 1. During that engagement, junta troops fired indiscriminately, killing two local civilians.
The weeklong operation forced residents from roughly 10 villages across Chaung-U Township to abandon their homes. Resistance fighters have advised displaced villagers attempting to return to exercise extreme caution due to the lingering threat of unexploded ordnance and landmines left behind by regime forces.

title: Fighting resumes in Sittwe as junta and Arakan Army exchange heavy artillery and drone strikes
body:
Clashes erupted between Myanmar’s military junta and the Arakan Army (AA) in Sittwe Township, Arakan State, on the morning of September 4, breaking a month-long lull in the state capital’s vicinity with intense exchanges of artillery, drone strikes, and ground fire.
Military sources and residents reported that active fighting broke out along the border connecting Sittwe and Ponnagyun townships. Regime forces deployed heavy artillery, multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), and combat drones, while AA forces retaliated with heavy artillery, drones, and small-arms fire.
“Tensions escalated after the junta launched provocative airstrikes yesterday,” a military source said. “Heavy artillery barrages this morning triggered mutual clashes, with both sides exchanging continuous fire throughout the day.”
The surge in ground fighting follows a series of junta air raids on the afternoon of September 3, which targeted seven villages across Ponnagyun, Sittwe, and Rathedaung townships.
The Sittwe front had been relatively quiet since late July before these latest strikes.
Residents in neighboring Ponnagyun Township reported hearing near-constant bombardments and small-arms fire from 5:00 AM to 10:00 AM on September 4.
“We started hearing heavy artillery, rocket launchers, and gunfire early in the morning,” said a Ponnagyun resident. “The clashes appear severe—the explosions were so intense that the ground shook in nearby villages.”
The escalation is part of a broader offensive by regime forces.
On September 3, junta warships shelled coastal areas in Gwa and Thandwe townships before launching coordinated air raids across Sittwe, Ponnagyun, and Rathedaung later that afternoon.
Following the intensified bombardments, the Arakan Army issued an emergency public advisory, urging civilians across Arakan State to take extreme precautions against ongoing naval shelling and airstrikes.
The AA has maintained a tight siege around Sittwe after capturing the surrounding townships of Werathani, Ponnagyun, and Rathedaung.
Although ground engagements directly inside Sittwe had temporarily lulled, AA forces have kept steady offensive pressure on regime positions through periodic artillery strikes and strategic encirclement.

title: Displacement exceeds 1.6 million in southeastern Myanmar as aid groups face mounting hurdles
body:
Escalating ground offensives and airstrikes by Myanmar’s military junta have displaced more than 1.6 million people across Mon State, Karen State, and Tanintharyi Region. Local humanitarian groups warn that fleeing communities face severe shortages of food, medicine, and adequate shelter.
Across southeastern Myanmar, relentless artillery shelling, drone strikes, and aerial bombardments have forced tens of thousands of families to seek refuge in forests and rubber plantations, where many have remained trapped for months.
“Data collected through August shows more than 299,729 people displaced in Mon State, over 799,700 in Karen State, and upwards of 516,240 in Tanintharyi Region,” said Nai Aue Mon, program director of the Human Rights Foundation of Monland (HURFOM). “In just one week, we confirmed an additional 2,500 displaced people in Karen, 1,200 in Mon, and 2,100 in Tanintharyi. The true figures on the ground are likely significantly higher.”
Humanitarian responders emphasize that displaced populations urgently require basic survival essentials, including tarpaulins, food, clean drinking water, medicine, and personal hygiene products.
The onset of the monsoon season has exacerbated health crises, with malaria, seasonal flu, and waterborne diseases spreading rapidly through overcrowded temporary camps.
“Almost every township now has displaced populations,” said a humanitarian worker operating in Tanintharyi Region. “They desperately need shelter materials, emergency rations, and essential medicine. Malaria is rampant right now, and we recently confirmed two or three deaths from the disease.”
The protracted displacement is also severely disrupting children's education and health.
Families living in primitive forest shelters report a lack of nutritious food for young children, leading to widespread malnutrition alongside limited access to schooling.
Safety risks remain extreme even when active fighting pauses. Junta forces frequently plant landmines near residential areas before withdrawing from military operations, posing a deadly threat to returning civilians.
Concurrently, humanitarian organizations face immense logistical barriers. Strict communication blackouts imposed by the regime hamper aid coordination, while relief convoys face harassment, arbitrary searches, and blockades at military checkpoints.
“Transportation is our greatest obstacle,” Nai Aue Mon explained. “Aid workers risk encountering junta columns or checkpoints at any time. Ongoing military operations, artillery strikes, and drone attacks make field distribution extraordinarily dangerous. Compounded by shrinking donor funding, organizing effective relief efforts is becoming harder by the day.”
The humanitarian crisis continues to deepen as regime forces intensify air and ground assaults in an effort to recapture lost territory, key border trade routes, and strategic positions across the region.

title: Death toll from Arakan State boat capsizes reaches 30 during monsoon season
body:
Fatalities from boat capsizing incidents in Arakan State have steadily risen throughout this year's monsoon season, with at least 30 deaths recorded between May and September.
According to local reports, the fatalities include nine residents from Anjanapura and Myebon townships, 12 from Rathedaung Township, and nine from Taungup Township. The victims include students, teachers, and other education workers.
In a recent incident on August 30, a motorboat traveling from Ohphauk Village in Rathedaung Township to Nyaungchaung Village in Buthidaung Township capsized in rough waters. Nine passengers were rescued, but a schoolteacher drowned.
The tragedy has renewed calls for enhanced safety measures on local waterways, where safety equipment remains scarce.
“All passenger motorboats should carry life jackets or plastic containers for emergency flotation,” said an education worker from Buthidaung Township. “Teachers cannot afford to buy life jackets on their meager salaries. It would be best if the United League of Arakan (ULA) could provide them.”
Travelers across Arakan State rely heavily on both land and waterway transport. However, since the resurgence of armed conflict in the region, land routes have been severely disrupted or blocked, forcing residents to rely on hazardous water travel.
As a coastal territory with extensive river networks, Arakan State faces heightened risks during the annual monsoon season due to sudden flooding, high tides, and powerful currents.
“During this period, extra caution is vital when traveling by water,” said a resident of Werathani Township. “Weather conditions are unpredictable, and river currents here are notoriously swift. Travelers should exercise extreme caution—such as seeking shelter in safe tributaries—when high tides coincide with heavy rain and strong winds.”
Local authorities and community leaders continue to urge commuters and boat operators to adhere to basic safety precautions to prevent further avoidable loss of life during the remaining monsoon months.

title: Youth-Led Initiatives Drive Inter-Community Cohesion and Trust in Arakan State
body:
Youth-led initiatives aimed at fostering social cohesion are gaining momentum across Arakan State through informal dialogues and cultural exchange platforms, bringing together young leaders from diverse ethnic and religious backgrounds.
In late August, approximately 100 youth participants—including Arakanese, Mro, Chakma, Khami, Muslim, and Hindu representatives—assembled in Kyauktaw Township for a cross-community networking event.
“The objective is to strengthen youth participation in the development of Arakan State,” said one of the event organizers. “We organized this to build closer relationships among local youth, with the ultimate goal of fostering long-term peace, stability, and development.”
During the session, participants engaged in open discussions, sharing traditional customs to bridge historical divides and build mutual respect.
Participants noted that these dialogues are yielding tangible improvements in inter-community relations, serving as an effective tool to reduce local friction.
“Muslim communities have historically coexisted alongside other groups in Arakan State for generations,” said Ko Maung Maung Than, a Muslim participant. “Opportunities to exchange cultural traditions significantly strengthen social cohesion. Sustaining these platforms will help reduce conflict and restore trust.”
While praising community-driven efforts, attendees emphasized that institutional support is equally vital for lasting stability. They called on the United League of Arakan (ULA) to prioritize minority rights and embed social cohesion strategies into its broader administrative policies.
“Officials serving under the ULA must pay close attention to ethnic minority groups and actively promote social cohesion,” said Ko Aung Lin, a Chakma youth representative.
Similar youth gatherings are now taking place regularly across Maungdaw District.
The Arakan Army (AA) has stated that building inter-community trust remains a key priority while actively attempting to involve diverse ethnic groups in its emerging administrative structure.

title: KIO Questions Nearly 200 PoWs Captured in Riverine Ambush Near Shwegu
body:
The Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) has initiated interrogations of nearly 200 prisoners of war (PoWs) captured during a high-stakes military operation targeting a junta naval flotilla near Shwegu Town in Kachin State, officials confirmed.
The captives were taken after the Kachin Independence Army (KIA)—the armed wing of the KIO—and allied resistance forces ambushed the 15-vessel regime convoy traveling upstream along the Ayeyarwady River. The KIO transferred all detainees to a secure facility before commencing investigations.
“They are currently under the custody of our military division,” KIO spokesperson Colonel Naw Bu said. “It is too early to specify the exact ratio of active soldiers to non-combatants, but everyone has been relocated to a safe location, and questioning is underway.”
Frontline KIA sources reported that approximately 190 individuals were captured, including 151 military personnel and conscripts, 17 police officers, 16 wives of military personnel, and six children, indicating that soldiers were traveling alongside family members.
The flotilla originally departed from Mandalay on August 21 to deliver critical reinforcements, ammunition, and supplies to besieged junta outposts in Bhamo Township. Upon reaching Shwegu in late August, the convoy faced intense bombardment from resistance forces as it attempted to push toward Bhamo on September 2.
Overwhelmed by the assault, two vessels raised white flags and surrendered to resistance fighters, while five other vessels sustained severe damage. Despite heavy losses, seven vessels managed to break through and dock in Bhamo on September 3.
The Ayeyarwady River remains a vital resupply corridor for the regime as it struggles to maintain control over Bhamo amidst ongoing resistance offensives across northern Myanmar.

title: Myanmar Junta Touts Post-Service Employment for Conscripts Amid Widespread Skepticism
body:
Pro-junta Telegram channels are aggressively promoting claims that private domestic and foreign companies are offering job opportunities to conscripts who complete their mandatory two-year military service.
Propaganda posts circulate job listings detailing salaries, overtime pay, and Social Security coverage, arguing that private firms—particularly security agencies—prefer hiring former conscripts for their discipline, physical fitness, and tactical training.
The channels also cite potential openings in lightning protection installation, street lighting, agriculture, livestock, and electrical manufacturing, often including contact numbers for security firms.
However, independent verification of these listings and company credentials remains impossible. Residents and analysts widely dismiss the campaign as regime disinformation.
“These are just claims made by the junta, not what’s actually happening on the ground,” a Mon State resident told Than Lwin Times. “In our area, we haven’t even heard of the junta discharging any conscripts. No one trusts these promises—it is nothing more than propaganda.”
The junta activated the People’s Military Service Law in February 2024, drafting young citizens across successive cohorts. To date, 25 batches have entered training, with the initial four cohorts having completed their prescribed two-year commitment.
Despite official claims that state ministries and private enterprises are coordinating post-service placements, junta officials themselves reveal a starkly different reality. The deputy minister of the junta-controlled Ministry of Labour recently admitted that only eight former conscripts from the first four batches have secured employment.
With each intake drafting approximately 5,000 recruits, the figure highlights the regime’s negligible capacity to provide post-service employment. Furthermore, the military administration has refused to disclose the total number of conscripts discharged, fueling widespread suspicion that high casualty rates on the frontline account for the missing transparency.

title: Seven Junta Vessels Reach Bhamo with Fuel and Reinforcements After Loosing Eight Vessels
body:
Seven vessels from a junta naval flotilla traveling upstream along the Ayeyarwady River from Mandalay have docked in Bhamo Town, Kachin State, according to local resistance sources.
The 15-vessel convoy originally departed from Mandalay’s Gaw Wein jetty on August 21 to resupply military outposts in northern Myanmar.
Despite coming under sustained attacks by the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and allied resistance forces along the river route, two riverine combat ships and five cargo vessels successfully reached Bhamo on September 3.
The arrival delivers critical resupply to regime forces in the area, delivering fresh troops, fuel, military supplies, and junta administrative personnel.
“The vessels have docked in Bhamo—two combat ships and five cargo vessels,” a Bhamo-based resistance fighter told NMG. “If this flotilla hadn’t made it, the junta troops here would have been in serious trouble. This time, the junta also brought administrative civil servants along.”
While the seven arriving vessels represent a smaller fleet than last year’s 13-vessel resupply convoy, local sources note that the substantial influx of reinforcement troops is expected to significantly impact frontline military dynamics around Bhamo.
The flotilla passed through Thabeikkyin, Tagaung, Tigyaing, and Katha townships before reaching Shwegu Town in Kachin State on August 28. After offloading portion of its cargo in Shwegu, the seven vessels resumed their journey toward Bhamo on September 2.
Meanwhile, heavy fighting continues upstream in Shwegu Township. On August 30, KIA and Kachin People’s Defence Force (KPDF) units overran a temporary junta security post near Zinbon Village established to guard the flotilla.
The regime subsequently launched a counteroffensive using four columns totaling roughly 200 troops, sparking active clashes across the Zinbon mountain range and along the Shwegu–Hsinhkan Road.
The seven vessels managed to slip through to Bhamo while fighting was ongoing, while the remaining eight vessels from the original convoy remain stationed in Shwegu.
Independent verification regarding the exact volume of weapons, fuel, and military hardware delivered to Bhamo remains pending.

title: Mon State Prepares to Expand Ethnic Language Instruction to Grades 4 and 5
body:
Preparations are underway to expand Mon language instruction to Grades 4 and 5 across basic education schools in Mon State starting next academic year, according to members of the Mon Literature and Culture Committee.
The initiative follows an August 26 meeting between officials from the military administration’s Ministry of Ethnic Affairs, the Department of Education and Ethnic Literature and Culture, the Mon National Education Committee, a Mon political party, and local literature and culture representatives to address Mon language education policy and regional schooling needs.
As part of the rollout, the Mon Literature and Culture Committee will conduct township-by-township assessments throughout September. The survey will evaluate current classroom conditions, student enrollment, faculty counts, and resource shortages across the state.
“As instruction progresses, we will make necessary adjustments to address emerging gaps,” a committee member said. “Our team will initially conduct consultations across all village tracts in Mawlamyine Township.”
While select schools with adequate faculty have already launched Mon language classes for Grades 4 and 5, widespread expansion is facing significant staff shortages.
According to committee members, no new Teaching Assistants (TA) or Language Teachers (LT) applied during the current academic year, primarily due to low incentives and lack of benefits.
To address the shortage, local Mon literature and culture organizations are mobilizing community teachers and attempting to supplement salaries and benefits through local fundraising. However, recruitment remains hampered by administrative delays between the Ministry of Ethnic Affairs, which oversees teacher appointments, and the Ministry of Education, which grants teaching authorization.
The upcoming Grade 4 and 5 courses will utilize Mon language textbooks and curricula originally developed in 2010. The committee is coordinating with the Department of Education to resolve ongoing textbook shortages before the new school term.
Mon ethnic language instruction is currently offered at basic education schools across six townships in Mon State: Paung, Chaungzon, Kyaikmaraw, Mudon, Thanbyuzayat, and Ye.

title: KNU signs off on designation of 33 ‘Kaw’ territories covering nearly 400,000 acres
body:
The Karen National Union (KNU) Central Executive Committee signed and approved the designation of 33 ‘Kaw’ territories covering a total of 380,984.1 acres in areas under KNU control on September 3.
The 33 ‘Kaw’ territories are areas governed under the traditional systems of Indigenous communities.
‘Kaw’ refers to a traditional territorial governance system that has existed among Indigenous Karen communities since before modern administrative systems emerged. Under the system, local communities protect, conserve and manage land, forests, mountains and natural resources in accordance with their traditional customs and practices.
According to KNU, 10 of the newly designated 33 ‘Kaw’ territories are located within the Salween Peace Park zone in Mutraw (Hpapun) District, while the remaining 23 are in the Thawthi Taw-oo Indigenous Park area in Tawoo (Taungoo) District.
The KNU Central Executive Committee said the recognition of the ‘Kaw’ territories aims to protect Indigenous communities’ land rights, ensure the long-term conservation of the environment, forests, water and land, and preserve the traditional cultural identity of the Karen people.
“By officially recognizing these ‘Kaw’ territories, local communities will benefit because they can manage their own territories, make a living according to their traditional practices and preserve their customs and traditions,” said Padoh Saw Lay Say, head of the Agriculture and Farming Department under the Central Executive Committee.
The signing ceremony to officially designate the ‘Kaw’ territories, held at an undisclosed location near the Thailand-Myanmar border, was led by Padoh Saw Eh Kalu Say, head of the Land Committee under the Central Executive Committee. Administrative authority over the territories will also be transferred to the relevant districts, townships and villages.
Each ‘Kaw’ territory is recognized as having its own traditional land-management system, governance by traditional leaders, and the authority to manage land, forests and natural resources in accordance with customary law.
Padoh Saw Eh Kalu Say said successive military dictatorships had refused to protect and promote Indigenous communities’ customary practices. In contrast, the ‘Kaw’ territories will be managed through the communities’ own customary practices and traditional governance systems.
More than 300 candidate areas have been proposed across Kawthoolei, the historic and aspirational homeland of the Indigenous Karen people, for recognition based on their existing systems of territorial governance and the protection and preservation of traditional customs. The KNU is reviewing the proposed areas before officially recognizing them as ‘Kaw’ territories.
The Central Executive Committee’s latest decision marks the second round of ‘Kaw’ designations. In 2022, the KNU recognized a total of five ‘Kaw’ territories in the first round — four in Tawoo District and one in Mutraw District.

title: Khumi Chin Community Opposes AA’s Arakan Language Curriculum in Paletwa
body:
Indigenous Khumi Chin leaders and civil society groups have strongly opposed the Arakan Army’s (AA) implementation of an Arakan-language curriculum in basic education schools across Chin State’s Paletwa Township, calling the move a violation of indigenous rights.
The controversy arose after the AA and its political wing, the United League of Arakan (ULA), introduced Arakanese literature and history as a mandatory Grade 12 subject for the current academic year—replacing the standard Myanmar language subject not only in controlled areas of Arakan (Rakhine) State, but also in neighboring Paletwa.
In a statement issued on September 6, the Global Khumi Organization (GKO) condemned the policy, stating that imposing an external ethnic curriculum without local consent violates the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP) and risks sowing deep communal divisions.
"Bringing a new Arakan-language curriculum into Paletwa, which is an integral part of Chin State, is seen as an attempt to exert dominant ethnic influence," a local Khumi resident told Chin World. "People are only remaining quiet because those issuing the orders are armed."
Developed by the ULA’s Arakan National Education Department, the new Grade 12 curriculum uses the Myanmar alphabet to teach Arakanese literature, history, and traditional customs.
While Khumi literature is already taught in predominantly Khumi areas, local communities view the AA's unilateral educational policy as an overreach of authority in Chin State, underscoring growing governance tensions between the regional resistance administration and local ethnic minorities.

title: Scammers Target Myanmar Travelers in Shan State to Fuel Telecom Fraud Operations
body:
Fraudsters in southern Shan State’s Taunggyi Township are targeting travelers at intercity bus stops and transit hubs, posing as bank representatives to collect national identification card (NIC) data and facial photographs for telecom scam syndicates, according to residents and victims.
Operating in towns like Aungpan, middle-aged scammers lure unsuspecting victims with offers to set up free accounts at major financial institutions, including KBZ Bank and AYA Bank.
After they take photographs of victims' identity cards and faces, the perpetrators abscond, selling the biometric and personal data to online scam operations—locally known as Zhapaian—for tens of millions of Myanmar kyat.
The scam exploits military junta travel mandates that require Myanmar citizens to carry physical identity cards at all times due to ongoing political instability.
Most victims realize their information has been stolen when they attempt to open a bank account themselves.
A resident of neighboring Ywangan Township, for instance, was turned away by KBZ Bank staff after finding an account had already been fraudulently registered using his identity credentials.
"I was in Aungpan when people offered to help me open a bank account. They took photos of my NIC and face, then claimed they couldn't finish it right away and left," the victim told the Shan Herald Agency for News. "When I later went to open an account myself, I was told one was already registered under my name."DOCX
Community members and cybersecurity advocates warn that stolen credentials put victims at severe legal risk, exposing them to liabilities involving illicit financial transactions, money laundering, and unauthorized loans.
Concerns are also growing over parallel security threats on regional transit routes, where individuals in junta uniforms have reportedly been seen photographing travelers' identity documents.
Local tech advocates have additionally urged the public to beware of phishing links distributed via Viber and Telegram platforms used to compromise mobile devices.

title: Key Myanmar Bridge Damaged in Junta Airstrike Amid Heavy Fighting Near Bhamo
body:
A strategic dual-use bridge in Kachin State’s Bhamo Township was damaged in a military junta airstrike on September 5, following heavy attacks by resistance forces on a military flotilla navigating the Ayeyarwady River, residents and resistance sources reported.
The Hsinhkan Bridge—which carries both a road and railway line linking Bhamo with Katha in Sagaing Region—sustained structural damage during the bombardment. The airstrike bent the supporting steel frame on the eastern side, left a car-sized crater in the bridge deck, and rendered the railway line completely unusable.
The attack occurred after a 15-vessel junta flotilla traveling upstream from Mandalay came under intense ambush by a resistance coalition, including the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and the Kachin People’s Defence Force (KPDF).
“The junta bombed the bridge both to secure the flotilla’s passage and to sever logistics routes coming from Sagaing Region,” a Bhamo-based resistance fighter stated on social media, noting that the narrow river section near Hsinhkan Village is a frequent ambush site.
While parts of the flotilla were heavily damaged—leading to the surrender of several vessels and the capture of nearly 200 prisoners of war by the KIA—seven ships, including two combat vessels, managed to reach Bhamo Town. Other vessels remain stranded in Shwegu Township.
Ground fighting continues to rage around Hsinhkan, Waema, Sinsakhan, and Nawngmo villages as disembarked junta troops attempt to regroup and counter resistance forces. Ongoing hostilities have restricted access to the site, preventing independent verification of the full extent of the bridge's damage.

title: Heavy Rains Trigger Widespread Floods in Kalay Near Indian Border; Thousands Evacuated
body:
Widespread flooding caused by days of relentless heavy rainfall has submerged low-lying areas across Kalay Township in Sagaing Region—located near the Indian border—forcing hundreds of residents and internally displaced persons (IDPs) to flee to emergency shelters and higher ground.
The Myittha River, alongside several key tributaries—including Nat Chaung, Aung Myin Thar, Sae Gyi, Nat Nan, Zin Ka Lin, and Upote creeks—overflowed its banks, inundating numerous rural villages and urban wards in Kalay town.
"With continuous rain, water levels are expected to keep rising," a local resident told Mizzima. "The eastern, southern, and northern parts of Kalay flood annually. Currently, only higher-ground areas like Tahan and a small section of the downtown center remain dry as the number of evacuees grows."
Floodwaters have submerged more than a dozen villages—including Phaungku, Kyi Kone, Nan Han Nwet, Nan Sawng Pu, Pyin Taw Oo, Sakhan Gyi, Taung Oo, Pyin Thar, Chin Saing, Hto Mar, and Zin Ka Lin—along with low-lying urban wards such as Mingalar Oo Yin, Nyaung Pin Thar, Aung Mingalar, Aung Thitsa, Aung Zeya, Nay Pyi Taw, Kyo Thon Pin, and Thazin.
The deluge inundated local infrastructure, flooding the Phaungku monastery, destroying a church in Khaikam, and sweeping away makeshift IDP shelters along the Myittha River. Authorities and rescue teams were also forced to evacuate several patients from Kalay General Hospital to safer facilities. Extensive agricultural fields and standing crops have been damaged, though full loss estimates remain unavailable.
Infrastructure damage has further complicated relief efforts. In southern Kalay, severed Ooredoo fiber-optic cables have left communities facing severe phone and internet blackouts, with repair crews unable to access affected sites due to high water levels.
Rescue operations are currently underway. Emergency relief centers, including one at Saint Mary’s School (BEHS-3) in downtown Kalay, have been set up to shelter displaced residents.
Local defense forces and administration officials are coordinating rescue logistics. An official from the National Unity Government (NUG) Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Disaster Management confirmed that response teams are assisting residents with household evacuations and navigating flooded roadways. Units from the Chin National Defence Force – Upper Chindwin (CNDF-UCR) are also actively assisting in search-and-rescue efforts.
The flooding in Kalay is part of a broader disaster unfolding across Upper Myanmar. Continuous heavy rains combined with dam water releases have impacted nearly 620,000 people across 25 townships in Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, and Ayeyarwady regions, as well as Karen State, leaving at least 32 people dead, according to NUG disaster response figures.

title: Arakan State Law Enforcement Faces Backlash Over Unresolved Rape Cases
body:
The Department of Law Enforcement and Public Security (DLEPS), the security wing of the United League of Arakan (ULA), announced that active operations are underway to arrest multiple fugitives wanted in connection with recent rape cases across Arakan State.
The incidents, which occurred in territory governed by the Arakan Army (AA), include the statutory rape of a minor in Werathani Township, the sexual assault of a woman with disabilities in Thandwe Township, and a fatal sexual assault in Paletwa Township.
The continued freedom of these perpetrators has drawn sharp criticism from women's rights advocates, who cite systemic law enforcement weaknesses, corruption, and informal out-of-court financial settlements as key factors allowing suspects to evade justice.
"The ULA must strictly safeguard the privacy and personal data of victims to prevent leaks. When such crimes occur, we want authorities to build solid, evidence-based cases for effective prosecution," said a female rights activist from Myebon Township.
Rights advocates noted that social stigma often deters families from reporting sexual violence.
They added that persistent telecommunications blackouts and severe transport restrictions in the region further hamper official investigations, giving suspects ample time to flee.
The delay in apprehending suspects creates significant judicial hurdles, according to local advocates.
"When perpetrators remain at large, critical evidence is lost, delay impedes timely data collection, and investigative tracking becomes far more difficult," said Ma Dar Li, an activist from Kyauktaw Township. "Leaking upcoming arrest plans and delays in reporting systems give suspects the window they need to escape."
Advocates are calling for comprehensive protection, physical and psychological rehabilitation for minor victims, and robust security guarantees for survivors and their families. While acknowledging DLEPS's ongoing efforts, activists emphasized that public anxiety will persist until the administration ensures fair, transparent, and timely judicial proceedings.
In response, DLEPS reiterated that the ULA is placing special priority on curbing child sexual abuse and pursuing maximum penalties. Under Section 376(3) of the applicable Penal Code, anyone convicted of raping a child under 12 years of age faces up to 20 years to life imprisonment.

title: Junta River Vessel Carrying Military Families and Officials Surrenders to KIA Near Bhamo
body:
A junta river vessel carrying military personnel, police, civil servants, and families of regime troops surrendered to the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) after coming under heavy attack along the Ayeyarwady River on September 2, according to resistance sources.
The vessel was part of a 15-ship military flotilla transporting troops, equipment, and administrative staff from Mandalay to Bhamo Township in Kachin State. As the convoy approached Hsinhkan Bridge, KIA and allied resistance forces ambushed the ships, forcing one vessel to raise a white flag.
Resistance fighters who inspected the surrendered ship reported finding military families, police, and civil servants intended to help restore the junta's local administrative machinery in Bhamo alongside displaced residents.
“Military families, police officers, soldiers, and civil servants were on the vessel,” a local resistance fighter told the Kachin News Group (KNG). “The junta seems confident it can restart its administration in Bhamo, which is likely why they brought along the required staff.”
Video footage obtained by KNG and shared on social media confirmed the presence of women and children among those who surrendered to resistance forces.
The flotilla—which left Mandalay on August 21 comprising riverine combat ships, bulk carriers, tugboats, and a sand dredger—had previously docked in Shwegu Township for five days before attempting the final leg to Bhamo.
Despite several vessels sustaining damage during sustained KIA ambushes along the Ayeyarwady River, resistance sources acknowledge that around seven intact ships from the convoy are expected to reach Bhamo soon.

title: At Least Three Civilians Killed, Homes Torched During Junta Raid in Chaung-U
body:
At least three civilians were killed, 20 others injured, and around 50 residents detained after a junta column raided villages across Chaung-U Township in Sagaing Region between August 29 and September 1, according to local sources and displacement workers.
The military column, comprising over 300 troops retreating from recent clashes in neighboring Monywa Township, shelled and opened fire on several communities as it advanced through the area.
On August 30, regime forces launched drone strikes around Kyeekan East and Kyeekan West villages, injuring nine civilians, while troops fatally shot a man who encountered the advancing column. The following morning, shelling in Khinmun Village killed a 35-year-old woman and her 70-year-old father instantly.
"Regime soldiers retreating from the Monywa fighting entered the village while firing artillery and small arms," a resident told Network Media Group (NMG). "An artillery shell hit the father and daughter, killing them on the spot."
The troops also set fire to Shwedarkya Village on August 31 and September 1, destroying at least 10 homes. The column continues to occupy the village while holding an estimated 50 residents who were abducted on August 29.
Local sources noted that the military raid followed an August 25 incident in which a local monastery abbot, accused of being a junta informant, died while in the custody of the resistance-run People’s Security Team (PST). Following his death, pro-junta channels called for military retaliation, prompting the deployment of the 300-strong column.
The violence has displaced nearly 8,000 civilians across 15 villages in Monywa and Chaung-U townships, forcing residents to seek shelter in nearby forests and hills amid ongoing daily clashes between junta forces and local resistance groups.

title: Thai-Myanmar Talks Gain Momentum as Junta Seeks Crackdown on Border Arms Flows
body:
Diplomatic and security exchanges between Thailand and Myanmar’s military regime have intensified following a visit to Thailand by junta chief Min Aung Hlaing, with both sides focusing on curbing cross-border arms trafficking and logistics for anti-junta resistance forces.
In late August, high-level Thai delegations led by the secretary-general of Thailand’s National Security Council and Thailand’s ambassador to Myanmar held back-to-back meetings in Naypyidaw with General Ye Win Oo, the military’s chief of staff.
According to junta state media, discussions centered on real-time intelligence sharing, border security, trade, and joint efforts to suppress illicit flows of arms, ammunition, narcotics, and precursor chemicals.
The diplomatic push follows an early August meeting in Thailand where Min Aung Hlaing requested Thai assistance in severing weapon supply routes along the porous 2,400-kilometer border, which spans Myanmar's Shan, Karenni, Karen, and Tanintharyi regions.
Military analysts and anti-coup figures warn that stricter border controls could disrupt logistics for resistance groups operating east of the Ayeyarwady River.
"Regions east of the Ayeyarwady River rely heavily on the Thai border for weapons and essential supplies," said Captain Zin Yaw, a former military officer who defected to the Civil Disobedience Movement (CDM). "With Thailand potentially tightening restrictions, resistance forces must explore alternative supply routes."
However, resistance commanders expressed skepticism over whether effective enforcement is feasible given the border's vast terrain.
"There are countless border crossing points," said Saw Dar Kou, a tactical commander with the National Unity Government’s (NUG) People’s Defence Force (PDF) in Tanintharyi Region. "The junta is attempting to project strength and cause hesitation, but resistance forces acquire roughly 70 percent of their arms directly from battlefield seizures during engagements with regime troops."
Thailand’s deepening engagement with the junta has drawn scrutiny from regional observers, as Bangkok has historically maintained working relationships with various ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) along its western border.
Beyond security talks, Thai officials also met with parliamentary leaders in Naypyidaw to discuss cross-border trade and joint measures against transnational crime, telecommunications scam hubs, and human trafficking.

title: Myanmar Junta Tightens Security and Imposes Restrictions in Ywangan Following Clashes
body:
Myanmar junta forces have intensified security checks, arbitrary arrests, and movement restrictions on civilians in Ywangan Township, southern Shan State, following a series of deadly ambushes and clashes with local resistance forces in late August.
Following fighting between Hstachan and Taungu villages in the final week of August—which reportedly inflicted heavy junta casualties—regime troops stationed themselves inside several rural villages across the Myaning Village Tract, including Ahlelchaung and Hpayargyikone.
Residents report that military personnel are enforcing an 8:00 p.m. curfew, banning public gatherings, and threatening to burn down communities if further resistance attacks occur.
"Junta troops were carrying out security checks before, but now they’ve become much stricter," a Ywangan resident told the Shan Herald Agency for News. "They arbitrarily arrest innocent people, and soldiers have warned that if fighting breaks out again, they will burn the villages to the ground. People are terrified of potential airstrikes."
Local sources also report that junta personnel operate in civilian clothing to conduct undercover patrols, arresting and interrogating individuals suspected of ties to anti-junta forces.
In more remote villages—such as Hsatchan, Taungu, Htaminpawng, Kyauktaw, Ngwetaung, and Thahpanpin—soldiers have reportedly detained and beaten local men, holding them without food until their families pay ransoms for their release.
The crackdown follows months of heightened instability in the region, including a major July 22 clash along the border of Ywangan and Thazi townships between regime forces and the Danu People's Liberation Army (DPLA), which left over 20 junta troops dead or wounded.

title: Cholera, Acute Watery Diarrhea Resurface in Myanmar as Severe Floods Displace 470,000
body:
Resurgent outbreaks of cholera, an acute watery diarrhea (AWD), have hit key regions across Myanmar, striking the same areas devastated by a nationwide outbreak in 2024, according to a report by the World Health Organization (WHO)-coordinated Myanmar Health Cluster released this week.
The disease resurgence coincides with widespread severe flooding affecting more than 470,000 people across 27 townships in Sagaing, Mandalay, Magway, Ayeyarwady, and Mon State. New cases of AWD are now emerging in flood-impacted communities in Sagaing, Mandalay, and Bago regions.
The current cluster began in Yangon on August 9, then spread to Sittwe (the capital of Rakhine State), Mon State, and the Ayeyarwady Region.
According to junta health administration data and health officials cited by international wire agencies, Yangon recorded nearly 500 hospitalizations and at least 150 confirmed cholera cases by mid-August, along with fatal cases reported in both Yangon and Sittwe.
Healthcare delivery across Myanmar remains severely crippled in the sixth year of civil war following the 2021 military coup.
The crisis has been compounded by chronic supply shortages, ongoing conflict displacement—including over 200,000 displaced people in Magway Region alone—and rising cases of malaria and dengue.
Concurrently, attacks on healthcare infrastructure persist at alarming levels. Between January and August, Insecurity Insight documented 101 attacks on healthcare personnel and facilities across the country, while WHO’s surveillance system verified 53 incidents over the same period.
Humanitarian agencies report reaching nearly 900,000 people across 330 townships with essential health services during the first half of 2026.
However, health partners warn that the recurrence of disease outbreaks in the exact locations hit in 2024 underscores persistent, unaddressed failures in clean water supply, sanitation, and disease surveillance.

title: AA Drones and Artillery Hit Junta Reinforcements Near Strategic Nat Yay Kan Base, Causing Heavy Casualties
body:
Arakan Army (AA) forces launched coordinated drone and artillery strikes against Myanmar junta reinforcements near the Nat Yay Kan strategic base in Magway Region on August 31, inflicting heavy casualties, according to local military sources.
The strategic base, situated on the Rakhine Yoma mountain range in Padan Township, remains surrounded by AA forces.
Multiple artillery shells exploded directly inside a junta column attempting to advance toward Nat Yay Kan near Pazhi village, injuring numerous soldiers and forcing the military to evacuate casualties by vehicle.
"The AA targeted them with drones and artillery, scoring direct hits on the column," a local military source told Narinjara News. "Wounded soldiers and bodies were transported back to Padan town. On the morning of August 31, supply trucks were repurposed to carry the casualties away."
A source close to the AA confirmed the evening ambush, noting that the AA relies heavily on drone surveillance along the strategic Ann-Padan road connecting Rakhine State and Magway Region to intercept troop movements.
"When movements are detected along the highway, the AA launches coordinated drone and heavy weapon strikes," the source explained.
Beyond drone and artillery bombardment, junta troops are suffering daily losses from close-range sniper attacks. Despite heavy casualties, desertions, and malaria outbreaks among newly conscripted soldiers, the military continues sending reinforcements to the area, including three trucks loaded with ammunition reported on September 1.
The junta has spent years attempting to break the siege on Nat Yay Kan using multiple columns, but AA resistance has halted their advance past the villages of Pazhi and Gok Gyi.
While a full-scale ground assault to capture the base has not yet materialized, both sides remain locked in intense artillery exchanges and drone warfare along the Rakhine-Magway border.

title: Foreigners Banned from Renting Homes in Lawngtlai District, Mizoram
body:
The District Magistrate of Lawngtlai District, a border town in Mizoram State near Myanmar’s Chin State, has issued an order banning foreigners—including Myanmar nationals—from renting residential properties, effective September 1, according to local sources and Arakanese traders residing in the area.
The decision was finalized during a joint security meeting attended by district authorities, representatives of the Assam Rifles, and the Central Young Lai Association (CYLA).
While informal restrictions on housing rentals for foreigners had been observed over the past three months, local traders report that official enforcement is set to tighten significantly.
"Previously, landlords and tenants arranged housing through mutual agreements. With an official ban in place, living expenses will escalate dramatically," said an Arakanese trader based in Lawngtlai.
Lawngtlai District, which borders Paletwa Township in Chin State, currently hosts tens of thousands of refugees who fled Chin State and Sagaing Region following Myanmar’s 2021 military coup. It also serves as a crucial hub for border traders from Arakan (Rakhine) State who established operations in Mizoram after cross-border trade expanded in 2024.
Traders noted that the crackdown stems primarily from growing concerns among Indian authorities over illegal drug trafficking originating from Chin State.
"Authorities are concerned about illegal drug trade by individuals establishing long-term residency," another trader explained. "Transient traders moving back and forth may not face major disruptions, but long-term residents will no longer be able to rent homes. Staying in hotels or guesthouses will prove financially unsustainable for many."
Alongside the rental ban, the District Magistrate warned that individuals caught using fraudulent documentation, forging papers, or making unauthorized border crossings will face immediate arrest and prosecution.
The housing restrictions are expected to severely impact the asylum seekers, commodity flows, and local livelihoods. Since the Myanmar military junta instituted blockades across Arakan State during intense fighting in late 2023, the region has relied heavily on trade routes through Mizoram for necessities, including food, medicine, and cooking oil.

title: War, Conscription, and Unemployment Threaten Future of Arakan Youth: Study
body:
A comprehensive new report by the Center for Arakan Studies reveals that young people in Arakan State face a bleak and profoundly uncertain future, battered by protracted conflict, forced military recruitment, severe travel restrictions, soaring unemployment, and systemic educational collapse.
Published on August 31 as Arakan Affairs Special Study No. 10 (2026), the report examines the compounding crises affecting youth from January 2024 through August 2026, building on the devastating impacts of renewed fighting between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army (AA) that erupted in November 2023.
The study details intensifying pressure from all sides. The military regime has aggressively conscripted youths—including Muslims in Sittwe and Kyaukphyu—while the AA implemented its National Defence Emergency Provision (NDEP) in March 2025, barring service-eligible residents from leaving Arakan.
Citing data from Unlawful Conscription Watch (UCW), the report reveals that the junta forcibly recruited 3,993 individuals from Arakan between May 2025 and May 2026—the second-highest conscription among the 15 States, Regions, and Union Territory tracked nationwide.
Concurrently, the study documents alarming incidents of youths being detained while attempting to flee AA-controlled territories, with over 80 arrested in Thandwe Township alone and subsequently funneled into military training.
Socioeconomic conditions have simultaneously deteriorated. Citing a Youth-Led Organization (YLO) assessment, the findings indicate that 55 percent of young people in Arakan are unemployed, crippled by a scarcity of jobs, widening skills gaps, and a total lack of startup capital.
Years of warfare have deeply fractured higher education, while stringent mobility restrictions and administrative barriers in obtaining identification documents effectively trap youth inside the state. Although alternative educational pathways have begun emerging in AA-administered zones through 2025 and 2026, systemic recovery remains out of reach.
The Center for Arakan Studies warns that an entire generation is being systematically trapped between active warfare, economic destitution, educational deprivation, and family hardship—a catastrophe with generational repercussions.
The report urges governing authorities and civil society organizations to urgently formulate robust policies addressing immediate safety and livelihood needs while establishing long-term sustainable frameworks for the region's youth.

title: Fierce Fighting Erupts Between Myanmar Military and Arakan Army on Strategic Mountain Route
body:
Intense combat has flared between the Myanmar military and the Arakan Army (AA) along the Arakan Yoma mountain corridor linking Rakhine State's Ann Township to Magway Region's Mindon Township, locally known as the Ta Lai Taung–Ta Phan Raung Road.
Clashes erupted on August 30 after regime forces launched a large-scale infiltration attempt.
"The junta army is advancing across the Rakhine Yoma in divided columns, and the AA is actively engaging these separated lines," a local source reported.
In response to fierce ground engagements, the regime has launched heavy aerial bombardments along the strategic corridor connecting Ann and Mindon via Ma Ei.
A military observer warned that travelers commuting between Rakhine State and Yangon should completely avoid the route, as encountering advancing military columns poses an extreme risk of arbitrary detention or death.
Daily fighting persists across multiple key locations along the mountain range—including the Nat Yay Kan air defense base, the Thaphan Raung bypass, Saw Township in Magway Region, and Nyaungyo in Bago Region—as the junta deploys thousands of troops in a major offensive.

title: Drafting Chinland Defence Law Emerges as Top Priority for Chin State Parliament
body:
The Chin State Parliament has prioritized drafting and enacting a comprehensive Chinland Defence Law to establish a unified legal framework for all revolutionary armed forces operating across the region.
Spearheaded by the Defence Minister of the Government of Chinland—formed under the revolutionary Chinland Council—the legislative effort brings together officials from the parliament, the Ministry of Defence, and the Defence Coordination Team (DCT).
“The Chinland Council’s DCT has tasked us with drafting this law. Given the complexities involved, we plan to utilize an interim Terms of Reference (ToR) approach to address immediate operational issues while revolutionary forces are being consolidated,” said U Hung Naing, speaker of the Chin State Parliament.
The interim ToR guidelines were dispatched in late August to the Chinland Council, the regional revolutionary government, and local administrative units.
Developing a universally accepted framework presents organizational and political challenges due to the diverse backgrounds of various Chinland Defence Force (CDF) factions formed during the anti-junta revolution.
To ensure consensus, the parliament plans to circulate the draft among all regional units, CDF factions, and the Chin National Army (CNA) for comprehensive review before final enactment.
Concurrently, the Ministry of Defence is pushing to unify the CNA and autonomous CDF factions under a single civilian command structure, a mandate guaranteed by the 2023 Chinland Constitution.
“Bringing all resistance forces under civilian oversight is essential. Right now, we are actively organizing battalions and units under the ministry,” said Salai Kep Chin Thang, secretary of the Chinland Council, which has established local administrations across 19 townships and regions as part of the nationwide resistance movement against military rule.
